audio.text: Most code that clusters vectors runs Lloyd's k-means. [[emeans]]Meta's new e-means promises the same result in a tenth of the passes. We measured [[where]]where that holds, and where it doesn't.

Lloyd's algorithm alternates two steps. [[assign]]Assign every point to its nearest centre. [[move]]Move each centre to the mean of its points. [[repeat]]Repeat, often twenty-five times, and every round reads all the data.

e-means reads the data in [[batches]]small batches. Each batch [[nudges]]nudges the centres with a moving average, and [[revive]]empty clusters are split off busy ones. Two passes usually land where twenty-five rounds of Lloyd do.

We timed both on sixty-one clustering jobs, up to a million points and sixteen thousand clusters. [[high]]With thirty-two or more dimensions and at least fifty points per cluster, two passes of e-means usually beat twenty-five rounds of Lloyd outright, and reached Lloyd's error at least one and a half to nine times sooner. [[torch]]Its PyTorch version, which also swaps in a faster search, was up to fifty-two times sooner.

[[few]]On our synthetic data, below about twenty-five points per cluster, e-means stopped at a higher error than Lloyd. [[three]]And on three-dimensional data like pixel colours, with a thousand clusters or more, it was slower. [[faiss]]The faiss search inside it costs up to fifty times more per distance on small batches there.

We built this for a [ColBERT](/kQlbˈɛə/) search index, which stores a vector for every token, and we shrink each one to a few bits, as an offset from [[mean]]one shared average. Offset each token instead from its [[nearest]]nearest of sixteen thousand centroids, and at one bit the ranking scores [[gain]]up to two points higher. That's about what a second bit buys.

The centroids have to be stored, though. [[table]]On a five-thousand-document collection, that table costs as much as the bit it saves, so the two tie. [[large]]A collection large enough to spread it thin would get the same quality in about a third fewer bytes. That last number is arithmetic, not a measurement.

And the trainer hardly mattered for search. [[lloyd2]]Two rounds of Lloyd, twenty-five rounds, or e-means: [[same]]the rankings mostly came out within half a point. [[faster]]e-means fit the centroids about twelve times faster than twenty-five rounds of Lloyd.

[[r1]]Reach for e-means on high-dimensional data with plenty of points per cluster. [[r2]]Keep Lloyd for small clusters and low-dimensional faiss jobs. [[r3]]And check whether your downstream metric even notices.
